intro: Welcome! At C1 you learnt to hear understatement, irony and the polite no. Now you go further: you decode the polite code people use at work ("I'm not sure that's the best idea" usually means "I disagree"), use it yourself when it fits, catch irony and litotes from the words alone, and read what an answer means by what it avoids.
teachingNotes: Recap in one line, don't re-teach: from c1-listening-implicit the learner already hears five patterns in the WORDS (understatement: It wasn't exactly a success; irony: Oh great, another delay; reluctance: I suppose I could; hedged refusal: Let me think about it; faint praise: Well, he's always on time) and compares words with facts; from c1-register they choose register by audience, channel and purpose; from c1-debate they know With all due respect often comes before strong disagreement and to acknowledge before countering. New at C2: (1) the polite code at work, decoded AND used; (2) irony cues, litotes and dry humour; (3) conversation subtext explained with Grice's idea in plain words.

The polite code (objective interpret-and-convey). Decode: I'm not sure that's the best idea = I disagree (the node's common error is taking it as real uncertainty); With respect, … = disagreement is coming; I hear what you're saying = but I don't agree / I'm not changing my mind; It might be worth looking at … = you should (there's a problem); You may want to double-check … = I think it's wrong; That's brave / a brave decision = risky, maybe foolish; I'll bear it in mind = probably nothing will happen; Perhaps we could consider … = I want this; British quite good = often only OK (American quite good = very good); British not bad = good. Test for code vs literal: real doubt asks for information (I'm not sure: when does testing finish?); code is followed by a reason against or an alternative. Say honestly that these are tendencies: context decides.

Conveying (also interpret-and-convey): be indirect when the relationship is at risk (declining a client's invitation, criticising a senior person's idea, pointing out a mistake, hinting: It's getting quite late; Is it just me, or is it cold in here?), but direct when a misunderstanding is costly (safety, deadlines, money, legal points). Pattern for polite disagreement: soften + reason + alternative (I'm not sure that's the best idea: testing won't finish until the 20th. Could we keep the original date?). BrE is more ironic and understated, often in a flat voice; AmE is more direct and more enthusiastic. Indonesian bridge: iya often = I hear you (not I agree), nanti dulu = not now / a soft no, boleh juga = that could work (cautious yes). Trap: an English speaker takes a polite Yes as agreement; if you disagree out of sungkan and say nothing clear, the message is lost.

Irony and understatement (objective irony-understatement), from the words only: positive words + a clearly bad situation (Lovely weather for a picnic, in a storm; Well, that went well, after a disaster), markers (Oh great, Just what I needed, Thanks a lot), over-the-top praise (I couldn't have planned a better start). Sarcasm = irony that mocks someone: warn that it can hurt. Understatement: It's not exactly cheap = very expensive; a bit of a problem = serious. Litotes (not + the opposite): not bad = good, not unattractive = fairly attractive (careful praise), not the brightest = not clever, hardly ideal = bad, not without its problems = it has real problems. Dry humour: after a disaster, I've had worse days = I'm coping / joking about it, not a report that the day was fine; teach it, don't test it.

Subtext (objective conversation-subtext): explain Grice's idea simply, without terms like maxim or implicature: we expect each other to give enough information (not too little or too much), say what's true, stay relevant and be clear; when an answer obviously doesn't, there's a message. Patterns: avoiding the point (Did you like my presentation? The slides were very colourful = no), changing the topic, a reason instead of an answer (I've got an early flight = probably not), a weaker word (Most of them did = not all; some = not all), not answering a yes/no question (We're reviewing all our options = no promise), too much detail (a clue to nervousness, not proof: don't test it). Indonesian does the same (Mau ikut makan? Aku baru makan tadi = no thanks).

Limits and grading: the app's audio is one calm TTS voice, so every listen answer comes from the words; never claim tone, stress or accent can be heard in the recording. Listen texts are one speaker, at most 300 characters, natural C2 English; two-line exchanges are written in the prompt. Accept the meaning, not exact words, and synonyms of the list word with partial credit. At C2 many readings are subtle: only test cases where the words and context leave one clear interpretation, and say that these are tendencies, not rules. Contexts: Jakarta, Bandung and Surabaya offices, startups, client meetings, British and Australian colleagues.

keyPoints.title: Decode the polite code, and use it
keyPoints.explanation: At work many people, especially British speakers, use soft phrases with a stronger message: I'm not sure that's the best idea = I disagree (not real doubt); With respect, … = disagreement is coming; I hear what you're saying = but I don't agree; It might be worth looking at … = you should, there's a problem; That's brave = risky. Real doubt asks a question; code is followed by a reason against or an alternative. Use it yourself when a relationship matters (declining, criticising a senior person's idea, hinting): soften + reason + alternative. Be direct about safety, money and deadlines.

examples.en: I'm not sure that's the best idea: the budget's already tight.
examples.id: Aku kurang yakin itu ide terbaik: anggarannya sudah mepet. (= aku tidak setuju)

examples.en: It might be worth looking at the costs again.
examples.id: Mungkin ada baiknya kita lihat lagi biayanya. (= biayanya bermasalah, sebaiknya diperbaiki)

examples.en: Launching in the rainy season? That's brave.
examples.id: Meluncurkan di musim hujan? Berani juga. (= berisiko, kurang bijak)

id.title: Pahami kode sopan, dan pakai sendiri
id.explanation: Di tempat kerja banyak orang, terutama penutur British, memakai frasa halus dengan pesan yang lebih kuat: I'm not sure that's the best idea = aku tidak setuju (bukan benar-benar ragu); With respect, … = akan ada ketidaksetujuan; I hear what you're saying = tapi aku tidak setuju; It might be worth looking at … = sebaiknya kamu periksa, ada masalah; That's brave = berisiko. Orang yang benar-benar ragu bertanya; kode diikuti alasan menolak atau usulan lain. Pakai sendiri saat hubungan itu penting (menolak, mengkritik ide atasan, memberi kode): lunakkan + alasan + alternatif. Soal keselamatan, uang dan tenggat, bicaralah langsung.

keyPoints.title: Irony and understatement, from the words
keyPoints.explanation: Irony says the opposite of what you mean: positive words + a clearly bad situation (Lovely weather for a picnic, in a storm; Well, that went well, after a disaster). Understatement says much less than the truth (It's not exactly cheap = very expensive), and litotes uses not + the opposite word (not bad = good; not unattractive = fairly attractive; hardly ideal = bad). Tone can help in real life, but British irony is often said in a flat voice: compare the words with the facts.

examples.id: Cuaca yang pas buat piknik. (diucapkan saat badai: ironi = cuacanya buruk sekali)

examples.en: The hotel's lovely, but it's not exactly cheap.
examples.id: Hotelnya bagus, tapi tidak murah juga sih. (= mahal sekali)
Desain barunya tidak jelek. (= cukup menarik, tapi tidak antusias)

id.title: Ironi dan understatement, dari kata-katanya
id.explanation: Ironi mengatakan kebalikan dari maksudnya: kata positif + situasi yang jelas buruk (Lovely weather for a picnic, saat badai; Well, that went well, setelah bencana). Understatement (mengecilkan) mengatakan jauh lebih sedikit dari kenyataannya (It's not exactly cheap = mahal sekali), dan litotes memakai not + kata lawannya (not bad = bagus; not unattractive = cukup menarik; hardly ideal = buruk). Di dunia nyata nada suara bisa membantu, tapi ironi British sering diucapkan datar: bandingkan kata-katanya dengan faktanya.

keyPoints.title: Subtext: what an answer avoids
keyPoints.explanation: The philosopher Paul Grice described the idea that people in a conversation cooperate: they give enough information, say what's true, stay on topic and are clear. When an answer obviously doesn't, there's a hidden message. Avoiding the point (Did you like my presentation? The slides were very colourful = no), a reason instead of an answer (I've got an early flight tomorrow = probably not), a weaker word (Most of them did = not all) or no yes to a yes/no question (We're reviewing all our options = no promise).

examples.en: A: Did you like my presentation? B: The slides were very colourful.
examples.id: A: Kamu suka presentasiku? B: Slide-nya warna-warni sekali. (= tidak terlalu suka)

examples.en: A: Are you coming to the party? B: I've got an early flight tomorrow.
examples.id: A: Kamu datang ke pesta? B: Besok aku naik pesawat pagi. (= mungkin tidak)

examples.en: A: Did everyone sign the form? B: Most of them did.
examples.id: A: Semua sudah tanda tangan formulirnya? B: Sebagian besar sudah. (= belum semua)

id.title: Subteks: apa yang dihindari sebuah jawaban
id.explanation: Filsuf Paul Grice menjelaskan gagasan bahwa orang yang bercakap-cakap saling bekerja sama: memberi informasi secukupnya, mengatakan yang benar, tetap pada topik dan jelas. Kalau sebuah jawaban jelas-jelas tidak begitu, ada pesan tersembunyi. Menghindari pokoknya (Did you like my presentation? The slides were very colourful = tidak suka), alasan sebagai ganti jawaban (I've got an early flight tomorrow = mungkin tidak), kata yang lebih lemah (Most of them did = belum semua) atau tidak ada 'ya' untuk pertanyaan ya/tidak (We're reviewing all our options = tidak ada janji).

guidedPractice.prompt: In a meeting, a British colleague hears your plan to launch the app without any user testing and says: 'That's very brave.' Does she think the plan is safe or risky? Answer in one word.
guidedPractice.hint: 'Brave' about a plan at work is part of the polite code: it praises your courage, not your plan.

guidedPractice.prompt: Make this more polite for a meeting with your director, but keep the disagreement clear: 'Your plan won't work.' Start with 'I'm not sure…'.
expected: i'm not sure that's the best idea
i am not sure that is the best idea
i'm not sure that's the best plan
i'm not sure it's the best idea
i'm not sure that will work
i am not sure that will work
i'm not sure it will work
i'm not sure that's a good idea
guidedPractice.hint: The polite code for 'I disagree' starts with 'I'm not sure that's…'. Then, in a real meeting, add a reason and an alternative.

guidedPractice.prompt: During a thunderstorm in Bogor, Sari looks out of the office window and says: 'Lovely weather for a picnic.' Does she think the weather is good? Answer yes or no.
guidedPractice.hint: Positive words + a clearly bad situation (a thunderstorm) = irony: she means the opposite.

guidedPractice.prompt: Pak Hasan says about a new hotel in Bali: 'The rooms are lovely, but it's not exactly cheap.' Is the hotel cheap or expensive? Answer in one word.
guidedPractice.hint: 'not exactly' + a positive word is understatement: it means the opposite, and often strongly.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rina: 'Did you like the film?' Budi: 'The popcorn was great.' Did Budi like the film? Answer yes or probably not.
guidedPractice.hint: Rina asked about the film. Budi praises something else and avoids the film: that's the message.

independentPractice.prompt: A client in Singapore invites you to dinner on Friday, but you can't go. Write a polite reply in one sentence that declines without saying 'no'.
expected: that's very kind of you but i'm afraid i've already got plans on friday
thank you so much but i'm afraid i'm busy on friday
i'd love to but i'm afraid i've got something on that evening
that's very kind but unfortunately i can't make it on friday
thank you for the invitation but i'm afraid i already have plans
independentPractice.hint: Thank them first, then use 'I'm afraid…' or 'unfortunately…' with a reason. You can suggest another time.

independentPractice.prompt: Bu Ani asks: 'Did everyone in the team like the new schedule?' Pak Hasan answers: 'Most of them did.' Did everyone like it? Answer yes or no.
independentPractice.hint: 'Most' is weaker than 'everyone'. If everyone had liked it, he would simply say 'Yes, everyone.'

independentPractice.prompt: A British colleague says your idea is 'not bad at all'. Does she think it's bad, OK or good? Answer in one word.
independentPractice.hint: This is litotes: not + the opposite word. In British English 'not bad at all' is real praise.

assessment.prompt: In a project meeting in Bandung, the CEO, Pak Rudi, suggests cutting the testing phase so the app can launch a month earlier. Listen to the senior engineer's reply. Which word best describes what she really thinks of his plan: supportive, opposed, undecided or confused? Write one word.
assessment.listen: With respect, Pak Rudi, I understand why speed matters. I'm just not sure that cutting the testing phase is the best idea. The last time we did that, we spent two months fixing problems. Perhaps we could talk to the quality team before we decide.
assessment.rubric: Correct: opposed ('With respect' signals disagreement, 'I'm just not sure … is the best idea' is the polite code for 'I disagree', and she gives a reason against and an alternative). A synonym not from the list (against, disagrees, unconvinced, negative) = 80. The idea in Indonesian (tidak setuju, menolak) = 60. 'undecided' = 0 (the node's common error: taking 'I'm not sure that's the best idea' as real doubt; she asks no question, she argues against the plan). 'supportive' = 0. 'confused' = 0 ('I understand why speed matters').

assessment.prompt: Your British manager, Claire, reads the report you've written for a client and says: 'Thanks. It might be worth looking at the conclusion again before it goes out.' What is she really asking you to do? Answer in a few words.
acceptableAnswers: the conclusion is not good enough
look at the conclusion again and change it
assessment.rubric: Correct: change / revise / improve the conclusion before sending it ('It might be worth looking at …' is the polite code for 'you should change this: there's a problem'). 'Look at the conclusion again' or 'check the conclusion' = 70 (the right part of the report, but it misses that a change is expected). The idea in Indonesian (perbaiki kesimpulannya) = 60. 'Nothing, it's optional' / 'send it as it is' = 0 (taking the polite code literally). 'She likes the report' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Your director, Bu Ani, is about to present to a client in an hour, and you notice that the dates on slide 4 are wrong. You want to tell her politely. Complete the hint with ONE word: 'It might be ___ checking the dates on slide 4 before the meeting.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: worth ('It might be worth + -ing' = a polite way to say 'you should check this: I think it's wrong'). 'wise' / 'best' / 'better' / 'good' = 30 (the right idea, but these need 'to check', not 'checking'). Any other word = 0.

assessment.prompt: Bu Sari arrives at the office in Jakarta after a heavy storm. Listen to what she tells her colleagues. Which word best describes how she feels: delighted, annoyed, grateful or relieved? Write one word.
assessment.listen: Lovely morning for a walk, isn't it? Forty minutes in the rain, no umbrella, and my ojek driver cancelled twice. Still, I've always wanted to meet a new client looking like this.
assessment.rubric: Correct: annoyed (irony: 'Lovely morning for a walk' and 'I've always wanted to …' sit next to clearly bad facts: forty minutes in the rain, no umbrella, a cancelled ride, meeting a client looking wet). A synonym not from the list (frustrated, irritated, fed up, unhappy) = 80. The idea in Indonesian (kesal, jengkel) = 60. 'delighted' / 'grateful' = 0 (the literal meaning of her positive words; the facts show the opposite). 'relieved' = 0 (nothing in the words shows relief).

assessment.prompt: Dimas, an analyst in Surabaya, is asked about a two-day training workshop he went to. Listen. Which word best describes the workshop for Dimas: boring, exciting, difficult or useful? Write one word.
assessment.listen: The workshop? Well, it wasn't the most thrilling two days of my life. The trainer read every slide aloud, word for word, and by the afternoon most of us were checking our phones.
assessment.rubric: Correct: boring ('it wasn't the most thrilling two days of my life' is understatement for 'very boring', and the facts confirm it: every slide read aloud, most people on their phones). A synonym not from the list (dull, tedious, a waste of time) = 80. The idea in Indonesian (membosankan) = 60. 'exciting' = 0 (taking the positive word 'thrilling' without the 'not'). 'difficult' = 0 (nothing says it was hard). 'useful' = 0.

assessment.prompt:
Read the exchange.
Rina: 'Can you come to my wedding in Medan on 14 June?'
Dimas: 'Mid-June is when we close the financial year, and my manager has cancelled all leave for that month.'
Will Dimas come to the wedding? Write yes, no or maybe.
assessment.rubric: Correct: no (Dimas doesn't say no, but he gives a reason instead of an answer, and the reason rules it out: all leave is cancelled that month). 'Probably not' = 100. The idea in Indonesian (tidak, tidak bisa) = 60. 'maybe' = 30 (he leaves no real possibility). 'yes' = 0.

assessment.prompt: A journalist asks the CEO of a company in Surabaya whether there will be job cuts this year. Listen to his answer. Did he promise that there will be no job cuts? Write yes or no.
assessment.listen: Job cuts? Look, what I can tell you is that we're focused on growth. We've got a strong team, we're investing in new markets, and I'm not going to comment on rumours.
assessment.rubric: Correct: no (he avoids the yes/no question: he talks about growth and a strong team and refuses to comment. If there were no job cuts planned, saying 'no' would be easy and good news). 'He avoided the question' = 100. The idea in Indonesian (tidak, dia menghindar) = 60. 'yes' = 0 (positive words about growth are not a promise).

material.title: The polite code: phrases that mean more

id.title: Kode sopan: frasa yang maksudnya lebih kuat

blocks.text:
Quick recap from C1: you already hear five patterns in the **words**: understatement (*It wasn't exactly a success*), irony (*Oh great, another delay*), reluctance (*I suppose I could*), the polite no (*Let me think about it*) and faint praise (*Well, he's always on time*). From the debate lesson you know that *With all due respect* often comes right before strong disagreement.

Now go further. At work, many people (British speakers especially) use a **polite code**: soft phrases whose real message is stronger. Learn to decode them:
- *I'm not sure that's the best idea.* = **I disagree.**
- *With respect, …* = I'm about to disagree with you.
- *I hear what you're saying.* = …but I don't agree, and I'm not changing my mind.
- *It might be worth looking at …* = You should look at this: there's a problem.
- *You may want to double-check …* = I think this is wrong.
- *That's brave. / That's a brave decision.* = That's risky, maybe foolish.
- *I'll bear it in mind.* = I probably won't do anything with it.
- *Perhaps we could consider …* = I want us to do this.

**Code or real doubt?** Look at what comes next. Real doubt asks for information: *I'm not sure: when does testing finish?* Code is followed by a **reason against** (*the budget's already tight*) or an **alternative** (*Perhaps we could start with Bandung*).

id.text:
Ulang singkat dari C1: kamu sudah bisa menangkap lima pola dari **kata-katanya**: understatement (*It wasn't exactly a success*), ironi (*Oh great, another delay*), keengganan (*I suppose I could*), penolakan halus (*Let me think about it*) dan pujian tipis (*Well, he's always on time*). Dari pelajaran debat kamu tahu bahwa *With all due respect* sering muncul tepat sebelum ketidaksetujuan yang kuat.

Sekarang kita lebih jauh. Di tempat kerja, banyak orang (terutama penutur British) memakai **kode sopan**: frasa halus yang pesan sebenarnya lebih kuat. Pelajari cara membacanya:
- *I'm not sure that's the best idea.* = **Aku tidak setuju.**
- *With respect, …* = Aku akan menyatakan tidak setuju denganmu.
- *I hear what you're saying.* = …tapi aku tidak setuju, dan pendapatku tidak berubah.
- *It might be worth looking at …* = Sebaiknya kamu periksa ini: ada masalah.
- *You may want to double-check …* = Menurutku ini salah.
- *That's brave. / That's a brave decision.* = Itu berisiko, mungkin malah ceroboh.
- *I'll bear it in mind.* = Kemungkinan besar tidak akan kutindaklanjuti.
- *Perhaps we could consider …* = Aku ingin kita melakukan ini.

**Kode atau benar-benar ragu?** Lihat apa yang datang sesudahnya. Orang yang benar-benar ragu meminta informasi: *I'm not sure: when does testing finish?* Kode diikuti **alasan menolak** (*the budget's already tight*) atau **usulan lain** (*Perhaps we could start with Bandung*).

blocks.text:
**The commonest mistake:** taking *I'm not sure that's the best idea* as real doubt, then answering with more details, as if the person only needs convincing, and leaving the meeting thinking they agreed. Usually it means **I disagree**. Ask yourself: did they ask a question, or did they give a reason against and an alternative?

**Tendencies, not rules.** The same words can be literal, so context decides. Someone who says *I'm not sure that's the best idea. What do you think?* may really be unsure.

id.text:
**Kesalahan paling umum:** menganggap *I'm not sure that's the best idea* sebagai keraguan sungguhan, lalu menjawab dengan detail tambahan seolah orangnya cuma perlu diyakinkan, dan keluar rapat dengan mengira ia setuju. Biasanya artinya **aku tidak setuju**. Tanyakan pada dirimu: apakah ia bertanya, atau ia memberi alasan menolak dan usulan lain?

**Kecenderungan, bukan aturan.** Kata-kata yang sama bisa bermakna harfiah, jadi konteks yang menentukan. Orang yang berkata *I'm not sure that's the best idea. What do you think?* mungkin memang benar-benar ragu.

blocks.prompt: In a meeting, your Australian colleague says about your plan: 'I hear what you're saying, but I'm not sure that's the best idea. Perhaps we could run a small trial in one city first.' What does she mean?
options: She agrees and wants to start soon.
She disagrees with the full plan and suggests a smaller trial instead.
blocks.explain: 'I hear what you're saying, but' and 'I'm not sure that's the best idea' are the polite code for disagreement, and 'Perhaps we could …' gives her alternative: a small trial. She doesn't agree with the plan as it is. 'I hear what you're saying' shows she understood it.

id.prompt: Rekan kerjamu dari Australia berkata tentang rencanamu dalam rapat: 'I hear what you're saying, but I'm not sure that's the best idea. Perhaps we could run a small trial in one city first.' Apa maksudnya?
id.explain: 'I hear what you're saying, but' dan 'I'm not sure that's the best idea' adalah kode sopan untuk tidak setuju, dan 'Perhaps we could …' memberi usulannya: uji coba kecil. Ia tidak setuju dengan rencananya yang sekarang. 'I hear what you're saying' menunjukkan ia sudah paham rencananya.

blocks.text:
Decoding is half the skill. At C2 you also **choose** when to be indirect.

**Be indirect** when the relationship matters: declining a client's invitation, criticising a senior person's idea, pointing out a colleague's mistake, or giving a **hint** (kode halus):
- *It's getting quite late.* = Let's finish now.
- *Is it just me, or is it cold in here?* = Can we turn the AC down?
- *I don't suppose you're free on Saturday?* = Could you help on Saturday?

**Be direct** when a misunderstanding would be costly: safety, money, deadlines, legal points, instructions. *The scaffolding isn't safe* is not the place for *It might be worth looking at the scaffolding*.

**Polite disagreement = soften + reason + alternative:** *I'm not sure that's the best idea* (soften), *testing won't finish until the 20th* (reason). *Could we keep the original date?* (alternative). The reason and the alternative make sure the message isn't missed.

id.text:
Membaca kode baru separuh keterampilannya. Di C2 kamu juga **memilih** kapan bicara tidak langsung.

**Bicaralah tidak langsung** saat hubungan itu penting: menolak undangan klien, mengkritik ide atasan, menunjukkan kesalahan rekan kerja, atau memberi **kode halus**:
- *It's getting quite late.* = Ayo kita selesaikan sekarang.
- *Is it just me, or is it cold in here?* = Boleh AC-nya dikecilkan?
- *I don't suppose you're free on Saturday?* = Bisa bantu hari Sabtu?

**Bicaralah langsung** kalau salah paham bisa mahal akibatnya: keselamatan, uang, tenggat, urusan hukum, instruksi. *The scaffolding isn't safe* tidak boleh diganti dengan *It might be worth looking at the scaffolding*.

**Tidak setuju dengan sopan = lunakkan + alasan + alternatif:** *I'm not sure that's the best idea* (lunakkan), *testing won't finish until the 20th* (alasan). *Could we keep the original date?* (alternatif). Alasan dan alternatif memastikan pesanmu tidak terlewat.

rows.en: That's very kind of you, but I'm afraid I've already got something on that evening.
rows.id: Baik sekali, tapi sayangnya malam itu saya sudah ada acara.

blocks.text:
**British vs American.** British English uses more understatement and irony, often in a flat, serious voice, so even Americans sometimes miss it. British *not bad* = good. British *quite good* often means only OK (lumayan), while American *quite good* means very good. American speakers tend to be more direct and more enthusiastic (*That's awesome!* may just mean *fine*).

**Indonesian as a bridge.** Indonesian has its own code: *iya* often means *I hear you*, not *I agree*; *nanti dulu* = not now, often a soft no; *boleh juga* = that could work (a careful yes). **The trap:** an English speaker hears your polite *Yes* as agreement. If you only mean *I'm listening*, say *I see* or *Right*. If you disagree but stay quiet out of sungkan, your colleagues will think you agree: use the code, but add a reason and an alternative.

id.text:
**British vs Amerika.** Bahasa Inggris British lebih banyak memakai understatement dan ironi, sering dengan suara datar dan serius, sampai orang Amerika pun kadang tidak menangkapnya. *Not bad* versi British = bagus. *Quite good* versi British sering hanya berarti lumayan, sedangkan *quite good* versi Amerika berarti sangat bagus. Penutur Amerika cenderung lebih langsung dan lebih antusias (*That's awesome!* bisa saja hanya berarti *oke*).

**Bahasa Indonesia sebagai jembatan.** Bahasa Indonesia punya kodenya sendiri: *iya* sering berarti *aku dengar*, bukan *aku setuju*; *nanti dulu* = jangan sekarang, sering berarti penolakan halus; *boleh juga* = bisa juga tuh (setuju dengan hati-hati). **Jebakannya:** penutur bahasa Inggris mendengar *Yes* yang sopan darimu sebagai persetujuan. Kalau maksudmu hanya *aku mendengarkan*, katakan *I see* atau *Right*. Kalau kamu tidak setuju tapi diam karena sungkan, rekan kerjamu akan mengira kamu setuju: pakai kodenya, tapi tambahkan alasan dan alternatif.

blocks.prompt: Your director proposes holding the team retreat in Bali in the rainy season. Most of the activities are outdoors, and you think it's a bad idea. Which reply is polite but still makes your disagreement clear?
options: I'm not sure the rainy season is the best time, Pak: most of the activities are outdoors. Could we look at August instead?
The rainy season? That's a stupid idea.
blocks.explain: Soften (I'm not sure … is the best time) + reason (most activities are outdoors) + alternative (August): polite, and the message can't be missed. 'Yes, Pak. Sounds good' is polite but says you agree. 'That's a stupid idea' is clear but far too rude for a director.

id.prompt: Direkturmu mengusulkan acara retreat tim di Bali pada musim hujan. Sebagian besar kegiatannya di luar ruangan, dan menurutmu itu ide yang buruk. Jawaban mana yang sopan tapi tetap jelas menunjukkan kamu tidak setuju?
id.explain: Lunakkan (I'm not sure … is the best time) + alasan (sebagian besar kegiatan di luar ruangan) + alternatif (Agustus): sopan, dan pesannya tidak mungkin terlewat. 'Yes, Pak. Sounds good' sopan tapi berarti kamu setuju. 'That's a stupid idea' jelas, tapi terlalu kasar untuk seorang direktur.

material.title: Irony, understatement and litotes: listen to the words

id.title: Ironi, understatement dan litotes: dengarkan kata-katanya

blocks.text:
**Irony** (ironi) means saying the opposite of what you mean and expecting the listener to see it. **Sarcasm** (sarkasme) is irony used to mock or criticise someone: it can hurt, so use it only with friends, if at all. In real life tone helps, but British speakers often say ironic things in a completely flat voice (and our audio is one calm voice too). So learn the **verbal cues**:
- **Positive words + a clearly bad situation:** *Lovely weather for a picnic* (in a thunderstorm) = awful weather.
- **Set phrases:** *Oh great*, *Well, that went well* (after a disaster), *Just what I needed*, *Thanks a lot* (to the person who caused the problem).
- **Over-the-top praise:** *Honestly, I couldn't have planned a better day* (after three disasters).

**Understatement** (mengecilkan) says much less than the truth: *It's not exactly cheap* = very expensive; *We had a bit of a problem* = a serious problem.

**Litotes** is a type of understatement: *not* + the opposite word. *not bad* = good; *not unattractive* = fairly attractive (careful praise); *not the brightest* = not clever; *hardly ideal* = bad; *not without its problems* = it has real problems.

**Dry humour** (humor kering): after something truly awful, a British speaker may shrug and say *Well, I've had worse days.* That's not a report that the day was fine: it's a joke that shows they're coping by making the disaster sound small.

id.text:
**Ironi** berarti mengatakan kebalikan dari maksudmu dan berharap pendengar menangkapnya. **Sarkasme** adalah ironi untuk mengejek atau mengkritik seseorang: bisa menyakitkan, jadi pakai hanya dengan teman, itu pun kalau perlu. Di dunia nyata nada suara membantu, tapi penutur British sering mengucapkan ironi dengan suara datar sekali (dan audio kita juga satu suara yang tenang). Jadi pelajari **petunjuk dari kata-katanya**:
- **Kata positif + situasi yang jelas buruk:** *Lovely weather for a picnic* (saat badai petir) = cuacanya buruk sekali.
- **Frasa tetap:** *Oh great*, *Well, that went well* (setelah bencana), *Just what I needed*, *Thanks a lot* (kepada orang yang menyebabkan masalah).
- **Pujian yang berlebihan:** *Honestly, I couldn't have planned a better day* (setelah tiga kejadian buruk).

**Understatement** (mengecilkan) mengatakan jauh lebih sedikit dari kenyataannya: *It's not exactly cheap* = mahal sekali; *We had a bit of a problem* = masalah serius.

**Litotes** adalah salah satu jenis understatement: *not* + kata lawannya. *not bad* = bagus; *not unattractive* = cukup menarik (pujian yang hati-hati); *not the brightest* = tidak pintar; *hardly ideal* = buruk; *not without its problems* = punya masalah yang nyata.

**Humor kering:** setelah kejadian yang benar-benar buruk, penutur British bisa mengangkat bahu dan berkata *Well, I've had worse days.* Itu bukan laporan bahwa harinya baik-baik saja: itu candaan yang menunjukkan ia tetap tegar dengan membuat bencananya terdengar kecil.

rows.en: The hotel's lovely, but it's not exactly cheap.
rows.id: Hotelnya bagus, tapi tidak murah juga sih.

rows.note: litotes: fairly attractive, said without enthusiasm

rows.note: litotes: the plan has real problems

blocks.text:
**Why say *not unattractive* instead of *attractive*?** Because it's weaker and more careful: the speaker avoids full praise. Indonesian does the same with *lumayan*, *tidak jelek* or *bukan tanpa masalah*.

**Two traps:** taking irony literally (*Well, that went well* = a success?) and taking understatement as small (*a bit of a problem* = a small problem?). Check the facts around the words: when the words and the facts don't match, believe the facts.

id.text:
**Kenapa bilang *not unattractive*, bukan *attractive*?** Karena lebih lemah dan lebih hati-hati: pembicaranya menghindari pujian penuh. Bahasa Indonesia juga begitu dengan *lumayan*, *tidak jelek* atau *bukan tanpa masalah*.

**Dua jebakan:** menganggap ironi secara harfiah (*Well, that went well* = sukses?) dan menganggap understatement sebagai hal kecil (*a bit of a problem* = masalah kecil?). Periksa fakta di sekitar kata-katanya: kalau kata dan faktanya tidak cocok, percayai faktanya.

blocks.prompt: Rina's laptop crashed just before her presentation, and then the projector stopped working. She says: 'Brilliant. Now the Wi-Fi's down too.' What does she mean?
options: She's pleased that the Wi-Fi is down.
She's frustrated: one more thing has gone wrong.
She thinks the Wi-Fi is brilliant.
blocks.explain: Irony: a positive word (Brilliant) next to a clearly bad fact (the Wi-Fi is down, after a crash and a broken projector). The facts tell you she's frustrated. The other two options take 'Brilliant' literally.

id.prompt: Laptop Rina mati tepat sebelum presentasinya, lalu proyektornya berhenti bekerja. Ia berkata: 'Brilliant. Now the Wi-Fi's down too.' Apa maksudnya?
id.explain: Ironi: kata positif (Brilliant) di samping fakta yang jelas buruk (Wi-Fi mati, setelah laptop mati dan proyektor rusak). Faktanya menunjukkan ia frustrasi. Dua pilihan lainnya memahami 'Brilliant' secara harfiah.

id.title: Subteks: apa yang dihindari sebuah jawaban

blocks.text:
**Subtext** (subteks) is the message under the words. The philosopher Paul Grice described a simple idea: in a conversation we expect each other to cooperate, that is, to give **enough** information (not too little, not too much), to say what's **true**, to stay **relevant** (on topic) and to be **clear**. When an answer obviously doesn't, the listener looks for a hidden message:
- **Avoiding the point:** *Did you like my presentation?* *The slides were very colourful.* The question was about the presentation; praising only the colours = I didn't really like it.
- **Changing the topic:** *Is the project on schedule?* *Have you tried the new coffee machine?* = No, and I'd rather not talk about it.
- **A reason instead of an answer:** *Are you coming to the party?* *I've got an early flight tomorrow.* = Probably not.
- **A weaker word:** *Did everyone sign the form?* *Most of them did.* = Not everyone. *Some* = not all; *I think so* = I'm not sure.
- **No yes to a yes/no question:** *Will the office stay open?* *We're reviewing all our options.* If the answer were yes, saying yes would be easy: so there's no promise.
- **Too much:** a long explanation nobody asked for can suggest the speaker is nervous or defending themselves. This one is a clue, not proof.

id.text:
**Subteks** adalah pesan di balik kata-kata. Filsuf Paul Grice menjelaskan sebuah gagasan sederhana: dalam percakapan kita berharap satu sama lain bekerja sama, yaitu memberi informasi yang **cukup** (tidak terlalu sedikit, tidak terlalu banyak), mengatakan yang **benar**, tetap **relevan** (sesuai topik) dan **jelas**. Kalau sebuah jawaban jelas-jelas tidak begitu, pendengar mencari pesan tersembunyinya:
- **Menghindari pokoknya:** *Did you like my presentation?* *The slides were very colourful.* Yang ditanyakan presentasinya; yang dipuji hanya warnanya = aku tidak terlalu suka.
- **Mengganti topik:** *Is the project on schedule?* *Have you tried the new coffee machine?* = Tidak, dan aku tidak mau membahasnya.
- **Alasan sebagai ganti jawaban:** *Are you coming to the party?* *I've got an early flight tomorrow.* = Mungkin tidak.
- **Kata yang lebih lemah:** *Did everyone sign the form?* *Most of them did.* = Belum semua. *Some* = tidak semua; *I think so* = aku tidak yakin.
- **Tidak ada 'ya' untuk pertanyaan ya/tidak:** *Will the office stay open?* *We're reviewing all our options.* Kalau jawabannya ya, mudah sekali bilang ya: jadi tidak ada janji.
- **Terlalu banyak:** penjelasan panjang yang tidak diminta bisa menandakan pembicaranya gugup atau sedang membela diri. Yang ini petunjuk, bukan bukti.

blocks.text: **You already do this in Indonesian.** *Mau ikut makan?* *Aku baru makan tadi* = no thanks. The trap is switching the skill off in English and waiting for a clear yes or no. And the other way round: when YOU avoid a question in English (out of sungkan), expect the other person to hear it as a no, or as a problem you're hiding.

id.text: **Kamu sudah melakukan ini dalam bahasa Indonesia.** *Mau ikut makan?* *Aku baru makan tadi* = tidak, terima kasih. Jebakannya adalah mematikan keterampilan ini saat berbahasa Inggris dan menunggu jawaban ya atau tidak yang jelas. Begitu juga sebaliknya: kalau KAMU menghindari pertanyaan dalam bahasa Inggris (karena sungkan), lawan bicaramu akan mendengarnya sebagai 'tidak', atau sebagai masalah yang kamu sembunyikan.

blocks.prompt: Sari: 'Is the new app ready for the client demo on Monday?' Budi: 'The login page looks fantastic.' What does Budi's answer suggest?
options: Probably only part of the app is ready.
blocks.explain: Sari asked about the whole app; Budi praises only one small part, the login page. A weaker answer than the question = the rest probably isn't ready. If everything were ready, he would just say yes. He clearly heard her: he answers about the app.

id.prompt: Sari: 'Is the new app ready for the client demo on Monday?' Budi: 'The login page looks fantastic.' Jawaban Budi menunjukkan apa?
id.explain: Sari bertanya tentang seluruh aplikasi; Budi hanya memuji satu bagian kecil, yaitu halaman login. Jawaban yang lebih lemah dari pertanyaannya = bagian lainnya mungkin belum siap. Kalau semuanya sudah siap, ia cukup bilang ya. Ia jelas mendengar pertanyaannya: ia menjawab soal aplikasinya.

Bahasa Inggris British dengan kecepatan penutur asli, latihan menyimak yang pas untuk level ini.

id.intro: Selamat datang! Di C1 kamu sudah belajar menangkap understatement, ironi dan penolakan halus. Sekarang kita lebih jauh: kamu membaca kode sopan yang dipakai orang di tempat kerja ("I'm not sure that's the best idea" biasanya berarti "aku tidak setuju"), memakainya sendiri saat cocok, menangkap ironi dan litotes hanya dari kata-katanya, dan memahami maksud sebuah jawaban dari apa yang dihindarinya.
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana aku tahu 'I'm not sure that's the best idea' itu keraguan sungguhan atau tanda tidak setuju?
Apakah understatement British sangat berbeda dari bahasa Inggris Amerika?
Bagaimana cara tidak setuju dengan atasan dalam bahasa Inggris tanpa terdengar kasar atau lemah?
Bisa beri contoh litotes lain seperti 'not bad'?

assessment.im-1: Dalam rapat proyek di Bandung, CEO-nya, Pak Rudi, mengusulkan memangkas tahap pengujian supaya aplikasinya bisa diluncurkan sebulan lebih cepat. Dengarkan jawaban insinyur senior. Kata mana yang paling tepat menggambarkan pendapatnya yang sebenarnya tentang rencana itu: supportive, opposed, undecided atau confused? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.im-2: Manajermu yang orang Inggris, Claire, membaca laporan yang kamu tulis untuk klien lalu berkata: 'Thanks. It might be worth looking at the conclusion again before it goes out.' Sebenarnya apa yang ia minta kamu lakukan? Jawab dalam beberapa kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.im-3: Direkturmu, Bu Ani, akan presentasi ke klien satu jam lagi, dan kamu melihat tanggal di slide 4 salah. Kamu ingin memberitahunya dengan sopan. Lengkapi kodenya dengan SATU kata: 'It might be ___ checking the dates on slide 4 before the meeting.'
assessment.im-4: Bu Sari tiba di kantor di Jakarta setelah hujan badai. Dengarkan apa yang ia katakan kepada rekan-rekannya. Kata mana yang paling tepat menggambarkan perasaannya: delighted, annoyed, grateful atau relieved? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.im-5: Dimas, seorang analis di Surabaya, ditanya tentang workshop pelatihan dua hari yang ia ikuti. Dengarkan. Kata mana yang paling tepat menggambarkan workshop itu menurut Dimas: boring, exciting, difficult atau useful? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.im-6:
Baca percakapan ini.
Rina: 'Can you come to my wedding in Medan on 14 June?'
Dimas: 'Mid-June is when we close the financial year, and my manager has cancelled all leave for that month.'
Apakah Dimas akan datang ke pernikahannya? Tulis yes, no atau maybe.
assessment.im-7: Seorang wartawan bertanya kepada CEO sebuah perusahaan di Surabaya apakah tahun ini akan ada PHK. Dengarkan jawabannya. Apakah ia berjanji tidak akan ada PHK? Tulis yes atau no.
